questions.question: Who among the following is considered the most powerful Chola ruler?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Rajaraja I**__.
 
 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**
 __ 
• **Rajaraja I** was considered the most powerful and influential ruler of the **Chola dynasty**, which ruled South India during the medieval period. 
• His reign lasted from **985 AD to 1014 AD**, during which he expanded the Chola Empire to its greatest territorial extent. 
• Rajaraja I was known for his administrative efficiency, military conquests, and contributions to art, architecture, and culture. He successfully annexed territories like **Sri Lanka**, the Maldives, and parts of the Deccan region. 
• One of his most notable achievements was the construction of the **Brihadeeswarar Temple** at Thanjavur, a UNESCO World Heritage Site, which exemplifies the architectural brilliance of the Chola era. 
• Under his reign, the Chola Empire became a major naval power, enabling trade and cultural exchange with Southeast Asia, including regions like **Java, Sumatra, and Malaya**. 
• His effective governance and military strategies laid the foundation for the prosperity and dominance of the Chola dynasty for several centuries. 
 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**
 
• **Other Options Explained:** 
• **Dantidurga:** He was the founder of the **Rashtrakuta dynasty** in South India. He ruled during the 8th century and was known for establishing Rashtrakuta dominance in the Deccan region. However, he does not match the legacy of Rajaraja I in terms of territorial expansion or cultural contributions. 
• **Harshvardhan:** A ruler from North India who belonged to the **Pushyabhuti dynasty**. He ruled during the 7th century and was renowned for his patronage of art and literature. Harshvardhan's influence was significant in North India but unrelated to the Chola dynasty. 
• **Virarajendra Chola:** He was a Chola ruler, but his reign came after Rajaraja I and was not as remarkable in terms of military conquests or cultural achievements compared to Rajaraja I. 
• **Chola Dynasty:** 
• The Chola dynasty was one of the longest-ruling dynasties in Indian history, with its origins dating back to the centuries before the Common Era. 
• It reached its zenith under rulers like Rajaraja I and his successor, Rajendra Chola I, who further expanded the empire. 
• The Chola rulers were known for their contributions to Tamil literature, art, and architecture, leaving behind monumental temples and sculptures. 
• The Chola navy played a crucial role in establishing trade routes and cultural connections with Southeast Asia. 
• **Brihadeeswarar Temple:** 
• The Brihadeeswarar Temple is also known as the **Rajarajeswaram** and is located in **Thanjavur, Tamil Nadu**. 
• It was constructed during the reign of Rajaraja I and is one of the largest temples in India. 
• The temple is dedicated to **Lord Shiva** and is an architectural marvel, showcasing the grandeur of Tamil temple architecture. 
• It is part of the "Great Living Chola Temples" recognized by **UNESCO** as a World Heritage Site. 
• **Important Points:** 
• The Chola dynasty laid the foundation for efficient governance by introducing the **village administration system**, which was a precursor to modern local self-governance. 
• Their contributions to Tamil literature, including works like **Silappatikaram** and **Manimekalai**, were immense. 
• Rajaraja I's reign was marked by significant advancements in art, architecture, and the establishment of a powerful navy. 
• The Cholas also focused on irrigation and agricultural development, ensuring economic prosperity during their rule. </ul

questions.question: After the Tughlaqs, which two dynasties ruled Agra until 1526?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Sayyids and Lodis**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Sayyid Dynasty (1414–1451):**

 
 
• The Sayyid Dynasty succeeded the Tughlaq Dynasty after the fall of Delhi to the Timur invasion in 1398.
 
• Founded by **Khizr Khan**, the Sayyids ruled parts of Northern India, including Agra, though they were relatively weak rulers.
 
• They claimed to be descendants of the Prophet Muhammad, which legitimized their rule in the eyes of many Muslims.
 
• The Sayyid rulers were not able to consolidate power effectively, and their rule was marked by frequent rebellions and the rise of regional powers.
 
 
 
• **Lodi Dynasty (1451–1526):**
 
 
• Founded by **Bahlul Khan Lodi**, the Lodi Dynasty succeeded the Sayyids and was the last dynasty of the Delhi Sultanate.
 
• The Lodis were of Afghan origin and significantly strengthened their hold over regions like Agra.
 
• **Sikandar Lodi**, one of the prominent rulers, founded the city of Agra in 1504 and made it an important political and cultural center.
 
• The dynasty's rule ended in 1526 when **Ibrahim Lodi** was defeated by Babur at the Battle of Panipat, marking the beginning of the Mughal Empire.
 
 
 
• **Connection to Agra:**
 
 
• Agra's prominence grew during the Lodi Dynasty, particularly under Sikandar Lodi, who established it as a key administrative and cultural hub.
 
• The Sayyids and Lodis collectively ruled Agra during the transition period between the decline of the Tughlaqs and the rise of the Mughals.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Sayyid Dynasty:**

 
 
• The Sayyid Dynasty had four rulers: Khizr Khan, Mubarak Shah, Muhammad Shah, and Ala-ud-din Alam Shah.
 
• They primarily controlled Northern India but were unable to expand their territories significantly due to internal dissent and external threats.
 
• Their rule weakened the Delhi Sultanate, paving the way for the Lodis to emerge as strong rulers.
 
 
 
• **Lodi Dynasty:**
 
 
• The Lodi Dynasty was the first Afghan dynasty to rule over Delhi and its surrounding regions.
 
• They implemented administrative reforms and promoted trade and agriculture to strengthen their economy.
 
• Sikandar Lodi was known for his architectural contributions, including the establishment of Agra as a major city.
 
• The dynasty's decline was marked by internal conflicts and the inability to resist Babur's forces at Panipat.
 
 
 
• **Historical Context of Agra:**
 
 
• Agra was an important city even before the Mughal era, with its significance growing under the Lodis.
 
• It became a key strategic location due to its proximity to major trade routes and its fertile surrounding regions.
 
 
 
• **Tughlaq Dynasty (Preceding Era):**
 
 
• The Tughlaq Dynasty ruled Delhi from 1320 to 1414 and was known for its architectural innovations and military campaigns.
 
• It fell into decline due to administrative inefficiency, rebellions, and the invasion of Timur in 1398, which severely weakened the Sultanate.
 
 
 
• **Battle of Panipat (1526):**
 
 
• This battle marked the end of the Lodi Dynasty and the beginning of the Mughal Empire in India.
 
• Babur defeated Ibrahim Lodi, bringing significant changes to the political and cultural landscape of Northern India.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Agra:**

 
 
• Founded by Sikandar Lodi in 1504, it became a prominent city during the Lodi Dynasty.
 
• It later became the capital of the Mughal Empire and a center for art, culture, and architecture.
 
 
 
• **Transition from Tughlaqs to Mughals:**
 
 
• The period between the Tughlaq Dynasty's decline and the rise of the Mughal Empire saw significant political instability in Northern India.
 
• The Sayyids and Lodis played a critical role during this transitional phase, maintaining the Delhi Sultanate's legacy until its eventual fall.

questions.question: The National Education Policy 2020 (NEP 2020) completed its 5 years in ______ 2025.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**July**__.
 
 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**
 __ 
• The **National Education Policy 2020 (NEP 2020)** was officially approved by the Union Cabinet of India on **July 29, 2020**. 
• The NEP 2020 aims to overhaul India's educational framework and provides a comprehensive framework for both **school education** and **higher education**. 
• Considering its approval in July 2020, the 5-year completion mark will fall in **July 2025**. 
• The policy has introduced several landmark reforms such as **multidisciplinary education, flexible curricula, holistic development**, and the promotion of regional languages. 
• The month of **July** is significant for NEP 2020 as it marks a pivotal shift in India's education system, aiming to align it with the **21st-century global standards**. 
 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**
 __ 
• **Salient Features of NEP 2020:** 
• The NEP 2020 emphasizes a **5+3+3+4 structure** for school education to replace the traditional 10+2 system, focusing on **foundational, preparatory, middle, and secondary stages**. 
• It encourages the integration of **vocational education** from an early stage, starting from Grade 6. 
• The policy aims for a 50% Gross Enrollment Ratio (GER) in higher education by **2035** and proposes a **Higher Education Commission of India (HECI)** as a single regulatory body. 
• It emphasizes teaching in **regional languages** wherever possible and the importance of **mother tongue** as the medium of instruction. 
• NEP 2020 introduces the concept of **Academic Bank of Credits (ABC)** to facilitate credit transfer and promotes **multidisciplinary education**. 
• **Implementation Timeline:** 
• The policy has a long-term implementation timeline, with some reforms such as the **common entrance exams for universities** already in progress as of **2023**. 
• Full implementation of reforms in school and higher education is targeted for **2030**. 
• **Key Reforms in Higher Education:** 
• The policy proposes the creation of large, multidisciplinary universities and colleges with at least 3000 students in each institution. 
• It aims to phase out the system of **affiliated colleges** and move towards granting autonomy to colleges and universities. 
• **Global Alignment:** 
• The NEP 2020 aligns Indian education policies with global standards by promoting **research, innovation**, and fostering international partnerships in education. 
 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**
 
• **Historical Context:** 
• The NEP 2020 replaced the earlier **National Policy on Education, 1986**, which was modified in **1992**. 
• It is the **third education policy** of independent India, following policies in **1968** and **1986**. 
• **Focus on Inclusivity:** 
• NEP 2020 emphasizes inclusivity by addressing **gender gaps**, promoting the education of **economically disadvantaged groups (EDGs)**, and ensuring access to quality education for all children. 
• The policy proposes the establishment of a **Gender Inclusion Fund** to assist in the education of **girls and transgender children**. 
• **Technology Integration:** 
• NEP 2020 highlights the importance of **digital infrastructure** and the use of **technology in education**. 
• It proposes the establishment of a National Educational Technology Forum (NETF) to enable the use of technology in education planning and learning. </ul

questions.question: How many female cadets passed out in the first-ever batch at National Defence Academy?

• A total of **17 female cadets** successfully graduated from the NDA, marking a historic moment in the academy's history. 
• This became possible after the **Supreme Court of India** in 2021 directed the admission of women into the NDA, ensuring gender equality in defence recruitment. 
• The female cadets were trained alongside their male counterparts, following the same rigorous curriculum that includes physical, academic, and leadership training. 
• The inclusion of women in the NDA is a significant step toward achieving **gender inclusivity** in the Indian Armed Forces.

 __

• It is the first tri-service academy in the world, where cadets from the **Army, Navy, and Air Force** train together before moving on to their respective service academies for further pre-commissioning training. 
• Established in **1954**, the NDA has been pivotal in shaping some of India's finest military leaders. 
• **Supreme Court's Directive for Women:** 
• In **2021**, the Supreme Court of India passed a landmark judgment allowing women to appear for the NDA entrance exam. 
• This decision was a step forward in ensuring **gender equality** and providing women with equal opportunities to serve in the armed forces.

• Female cadets undergo the same training regimen as their male counterparts, including obstacle courses, weapon training, and tactical exercises.

• This initiative aligns with global trends where women are actively participating in defence and security roles in various countries.

• **Historical Context:** 
• Prior to 2021, women were not eligible to join the NDA and could only enter the armed forces through other routes, such as the Officers Training Academy (OTA) or Short Service Commission (SSC). 
• The Supreme Court's directive was a landmark moment in the history of India's defence recruitment policies. 
• **Eligibility for Women in NDA:** 
• Women candidates must meet the same eligibility criteria as men, including age, educational qualifications, and physical standards. 
• They must pass the NDA entrance examination conducted by the Union Public Service Commission (**UPSC**). 
• **Global Perspective:** 
• Countries like the **United States**, **United Kingdom**, and **Israel** have long included women in their armed forces, with many serving in combat roles.

• **Protective Textiles:** Provide protection against hazards like fire, chemicals, and extreme temperatures, essential for defense and industrial sectors.

 __

• The index is structured around **four pillars**: Policy, Business Ecosystem, Export Ecosystem, and Export Performance. 
• **Gujarat** topped the rankings in the inaugural edition of the EPI 2020, followed by Maharashtra and Tamil Nadu.

• To examine the performance of Indian states and UTs in enhancing **export competitiveness**. 
• To identify challenges and opportunities to improve state-wise and national **export performance**. 
• To provide a framework for policy-makers to design and implement export strategies at the **sub-national level**. 
• **Four Pillars of the Index:** 
• **Policy:** Examines the export-related policies of states and their effectiveness in promoting exports. 
• **Business Ecosystem:** Evaluates the ease of doing business, infrastructure, and the availability of a supportive ecosystem for industries.

• **Export Performance:** Analyzes the export trends and growth from the respective states and UTs.

• **Significance of the Index:** 
• Helps identify bottlenecks in state-level export promotion strategies. 
• Encourages states to develop **export-oriented policies** tailored to their unique strengths. 
• Supports the central government's vision of making India a **global export hub**.

• **India’s Export Performance:**

questions.question: The first senior National Handball Championship was held at Rohtak (Haryana) in ______.

 __

They criticized the Moderates for their approach of petitioning and praying to the British government for reforms instead of taking assertive actions. ***Hence, all three leaders are correct.*** 
• The Moderates followed a strategy of peaceful and constitutional methods like petitions, resolutions, speeches, and delegations to achieve their objectives. This was referred to as the "politics of prayer" by their critics. 
• **Bepin Chandra Pal:** He was a key figure in the Extremist movement and believed in direct action rather than relying on constitutional methods. Pal criticized the Moderates for their lack of urgency and assertiveness. ***Statement I is correct.*** 
• **Bal Gangadhar Tilak:** He advocated for Swaraj (self-rule) and was a proponent of aggressive nationalism. He was one of the most vocal critics of the Moderates and called for mass mobilization and active resistance against colonial rule. ***Statement II is correct.*** 
• **Lala Lajpat Rai:** Known as the "Lion of Punjab," Rai supported the idea of direct action and criticized the Moderates for their reliance on petitions and negotiations with the British. ***Statement III is correct.*** 
 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**
 __ 
• **Moderates:** 
• The Moderates were a faction within the Indian National Congress during its early years (1885–1905). 
• They believed in constitutional methods to achieve political reforms and sought cooperation with the British government. 
• Prominent leaders included **Dadabhai Naoroji**, **Gopal Krishna Gokhale**, and **Pherozeshah Mehta**. 
• Their methods included drafting petitions, presenting memorandums, and holding discussions with British officials. 
• **Extremists:** 
• The Extremists emerged as a faction within the Congress after 1905, advocating for more radical methods to achieve independence. 
• They believed that the Moderates' methods were ineffective and promoted mass mobilization, boycotts, and Swadeshi (self-reliance). 
• Prominent leaders included **Bepin Chandra Pal**, **Bal Gangadhar Tilak**, and **Lala Lajpat Rai**. 
• They were instrumental in the Swadeshi Movement, especially after the partition of Bengal in 1905. 
• **Key Differences Between Moderates and Extremists:** 
• **Moderates:** Believed in gradual reforms through dialogue, cooperation, and constitutional methods. 
• **Extremists:** Advocated for immediate and complete independence using mass mobilization and direct action. 
• **Partition of Bengal (1905):** 
• The partition of Bengal by Lord Curzon in 1905 was a major turning point in the Indian National Movement. 
• It led to the rise of the Swadeshi Movement and increased support for the Extremists. 
• The movement focused on boycotting British goods and promoting indigenous industries. 
 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**
 
• **Formation of Indian National Congress:** The Congress was established in **1885** by **A.O. Hume** with the aim of providing a platform for political dialogue and reform. 
• **Swadeshi Movement:** Initiated in **1905** as a response to the partition of Bengal, it focused on self-reliance and boycotting British products. 
• **Extremist Leaders:** Known as the "Lal-Bal-Pal" trio, **Lala Lajpat Rai**, **Bal Gangadhar Tilak**, and **Bepin Chandra Pal** played a crucial role in shaping the Indian independence movement. 
• **Delhi Durbar (1903):** Held by Lord Curzon to celebrate the coronation of King Edward VII, it showcased the British imperial authority and further alienated Indian sentiments.

questions.question: Which article of the Indian Constitution is related with the Duty of the Union to protect States against external aggression and internal disturbance?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Article 355**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

 
• **Article 355** of the **Indian Constitution** states that it is the **Duty of the Union** to protect every state against **external aggression** and **internal disturbance**.
 
• This Article is a part of the **emergency provisions** under Part XVIII of the Constitution.
 
• The Article empowers the **central government** to ensure that the governance of states is carried out in accordance with the provisions of the Constitution.
 
• It provides the framework for intervention by the Union government in case of crises such as **riots, insurgency, or failure of constitutional machinery** in a state.
 
• Article 355 is closely linked with the imposition of **President’s Rule under Article 356**, which can be invoked if the state government fails to uphold constitutional norms.</li&

questions.question: During 1911-1921, what kind of population growth was recorded in India?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Negative population growth**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• During the period of **1911-1921**, India experienced **negative population growth**, which was an unusual demographic trend in the nation's history.
 
• This decline in population was primarily due to the occurrence of several **major epidemics** like the **1918 Spanish Flu**, which caused widespread fatalities.
 
• Other contributing factors included **high mortality rates** due to famine, poor healthcare infrastructure, and lack of effective measures to control diseases.
 
• The **Spanish Flu pandemic** alone is estimated to have killed over **12-17 million people** in India, making it one of the deadliest events during this decade.
 
• This period marked a sharp deviation from the usual steady or slightly increasing population growth rates observed in the preceding and subsequent decades.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Spanish Flu Pandemic (1918-1920):**

 
 
• The Spanish Flu was a global influenza pandemic that struck during 1918-1920 and is considered one of the deadliest pandemics in human history.
 
• In India, the Spanish Flu was referred to as the "**Bombay Fever**," as it first appeared in the Bombay Presidency.
 
• It led to the deaths of approximately **6% of the Indian population**, severely impacting the demographic structure.
 
 
 
• **High Mortality Rates:**
 
 
• India during this period lacked sufficient healthcare facilities to tackle widespread diseases effectively.
 
• Recurring famines, poor sanitation, and limited access to clean water exacerbated the situation.
 
 
 
• **Famine and Malnutrition:**
 
 
• Frequent famines, such as the **Bengal Famine of 1918**, further contributed to high mortality rates.
 
• Malnutrition weakened the population, making them more vulnerable to diseases like influenza and cholera.
 
 
 
• **Demographic Trends During 1911-1921:**
 
 
• This decade remains the only one in modern Indian history where **negative population growth** was recorded.
 
• After 1921, population growth resumed at a steady pace, marking the beginning of a new demographic phase in India.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Pre-1921 Population Trends:**

 
 
• Before 1921, India's population growth was relatively stable, albeit slow, due to high birth and death rates.
 
• This trend changed post-1921, as public health measures improved, leading to a gradual decline in mortality rates.
 
 
 
• **Post-1921 Demographics:**
 
 
• 1921 is often referred to as the "**Year of the Great Divide**" in Indian demography, as it marked the transition from fluctuating population growth to a consistent increase.
 
• This shift was driven by better medical advancements, improved sanitation, and famine control measures implemented by the colonial government.
 
 
 
• **Economic Impact:**
 
 
• The declining population during 1911-1921 also affected India's labor force and agricultural productivity.
 
• Recovery in subsequent decades required significant efforts in healthcare and disaster management.

questions.question:
Which of the following tax (now replaced by GST) was levied by Central government?

I. Entertainment tax

II. Entry tax
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**4. Neither I nor II**__.
 
 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**
 __ 
• **Entertainment Tax**: 
• Entertainment Tax was a tax levied on financial transactions related to entertainment activities such as movies, amusement parks, exhibitions, etc. 
• This tax was primarily collected by the **state governments** and varied across states in India. 
• Since it was under the purview of the state governments, the central government did not levy this tax. ***Hence, statement I is incorrect.*** 
• **Entry Tax**: 
• Entry Tax was imposed on the movement of goods from one state to another and was levied by the **state governments** to regulate trade and commerce. 
• It was not a tax imposed by the central government but by the states to protect local industries. 
• With the implementation of the Goods and Services Tax (**GST**), Entry Tax has been subsumed under GST. ***Hence, statement II is also incorrect.*** 
• **GST Implementation**: 
• The **Goods and Services Tax (GST)**, implemented in **2017**, replaced multiple indirect taxes, including both Entertainment Tax and Entry Tax. 
• GST is a unified tax system that is levied by both the central and state governments through the mechanism of CGST, SGST, and IGST. 
• **Central Government Taxes Pre-GST**: 
• Before GST, the central government levied taxes such as Excise Duty, Service Tax, and Customs Duty, among others. 
• Neither Entertainment Tax nor Entry Tax was under the central government’s purview. 
• **Final Answer**: Neither Entertainment Tax nor Entry Tax was levied by the central government. Both were state taxes, and they have been subsumed under GST. ***Hence, the correct answer is "4. Neither I nor II."*** 
 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**
 __ 
• **Goods and Services Tax (GST):** 
• GST is a comprehensive indirect tax on the manufacture, sale, and consumption of goods and services throughout India. 
• It was introduced on **1st July 2017**, replacing a plethora of central and state taxes. 
• GST is structured as a **dual system**, with the central government levying CGST (Central GST) and the state governments levying SGST (State GST) on intra-state supplies. 
• For inter-state supplies, the central government levies IGST (Integrated GST). 
• **Key Taxes Subsumed Under GST:** 
• Central Taxes: Excise Duty, Service Tax, Countervailing Duty (CVD), and Special Additional Duty of Customs (SAD). 
• State Taxes: VAT, Entertainment Tax, Entry Tax, Luxury Tax, and Octroi. 
• **Benefits of GST:** 
• It simplified the tax structure by replacing multiple indirect taxes with a single unified tax. 
• GST reduced the cascading effect of taxes, thereby lowering the overall tax burden on consumers. 
• It improved ease of doing business and increased tax compliance by implementing a transparent system. 
• **Important Constitutional Amendments:** 
• The implementation of GST required the **101st Constitutional Amendment Act**. 
• This amendment introduced key provisions such as Article **246A** (empowering both Parliament and state legislatures to make laws on GST) and Article **279A** (establishing the GST Council). 
• **GST Council:** 
• The GST Council is a constitutional body chaired by the **Union Finance Minister**, with state finance ministers as members. 
• It is responsible for making recommendations on tax rates, exemptions, and other policy matters related to GST. 
 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**
 
• **Role of GST in Tax Reforms:** 
• GST is often regarded as a **landmark tax reform** in India’s economic history. 
• It replaced a fragmented tax structure with a **single national tax**, fostering a common market. 
• **Challenges in GST Implementation:** 
• Initial issues such as technical glitches in the GST Network (GSTN) portal and compliance complexity faced by small businesses. 
• Despite challenges, GST has significantly enhanced **tax transparency** and compliance. 
• **Future Outlook:** 
• The government is continuously refining the GST structure to address concerns and improve efficiency. 
• Reduced compliance burden and uniform tax structure are expected to further boost **economic growth**.

questions.question: ____ was an ambassador who was sent to the court of Chandragupta by the Greek ruler of West Asia.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Megasthenes**__.
 
 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**
 __ 
• **Megasthenes** was a Greek historian and ambassador sent by **Seleucus I Nicator**, the Greek ruler of West Asia, to the court of **Chandragupta Maurya** in Pataliputra (modern-day Patna). 
• He is best known for his work **‘Indica’**, a detailed account of Mauryan administration, society, economy, and culture during Chandragupta’s reign. 
• Megasthenes’ observations provide valuable insights into the political and administrative setup of the Mauryan Empire, which included a well-organized bureaucracy and a strong central government. 
• He described the capital city of Pataliputra as a well-fortified and prosperous urban center, highlighting its grandeur and strategic importance in ancient India. 
• The work of Megasthenes forms one of the earliest sources of information on ancient Indian civilization, making his accounts an essential historical resource. 
 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**
 __ 
• **Chandragupta Maurya:** 
• He was the founder of the **Mauryan Empire** in 321 BCE and ruled until 297 BCE. 
• Chandragupta unified most of the Indian subcontinent, creating one of the largest empires in Indian history. 
• He was mentored by **Chanakya (Kautilya)**, the author of the **Arthashastra**, a treatise on statecraft, economy, and military strategy. 
• **Indica by Megasthenes:** 
• The work provides an account of Indian society, including descriptions of the caste system, religious practices, and urban planning. 
• Though the original text of Indica is lost, fragments and summaries of it are preserved in the works of later writers such as Strabo, Arrian, and Diodorus Siculus. 
• **Seleucus I Nicator:** 
• He was one of Alexander the Great’s generals and later established the **Seleucid Empire** in West Asia after Alexander’s death. 
• Seleucus entered into an alliance with Chandragupta Maurya, ceding territories in exchange for 500 war elephants, which played a significant role in his campaigns. 
• **Other Travelers to India:** 
• **Al-Biruni:** A Persian scholar who traveled to India in the 11th century and wrote the famous work **‘Kitab al-Hind’**, detailing Indian culture, religion, and science. 
• **Ibn Battuta:** A Moroccan traveler who visited India during the reign of Muhammad bin Tughlaq in the 14th century and wrote about his observations in his work **‘Rihla’**. 
• **Marco Polo:** A Venetian traveler who visited India in the late 13th century and described the country’s wealth, trade, and culture in his accounts. 
 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**
 
• **Megasthenes’ Indica:** 
• Provides one of the earliest descriptions of the caste system in India, including the division of society into seven classes. 
• Highlights the importance of agriculture, trade, and commerce in the Mauryan economy. 
• Mentions the absence of slavery in Indian society, which was a notable contrast to Greek and Roman societies. 
• Details the Mauryan administrative system, including the role of officials, taxation, and military organization. 
• **Legacy of the Mauryan Empire:** 
• The Mauryan Empire set the foundation for centralized governance and administration in India. 
• Chandragupta’s reign marked the beginning of a united India, with Pataliputra as its political and cultural center. 
• The influence of Mauryan policies and governance can be seen in later Indian empires.
